#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for which hosts get waypipe, the Wayland forwarding proxy in home.nix's
# home.packages.
#
# What is being protected here is a *pair*, and that is the whole point. waypipe
# is not a tool a host uses alone: `waypipe ssh <host> <app>` runs one waypipe
# locally, next to the compositor that will show the window, and a second one on
# the far end, next to the application. Neither half is any use without the
# other, so "which hosts have waypipe" is really "which hosts can be either end
# of a forward", and a gate that drifts to one host is a gate that has silently
# turned the feature off.
#
# Both halves also have to be the SAME waypipe. The 0.10 rewrite (C -> Rust)
# changed the wire format, and waypipe refuses a version mismatch rather than
# degrading -- so the two ends agreeing is a property of them coming from one
# flake.lock, which is exactly what the version case at the end asserts.
#
# The teeth at the end are about the cases themselves: a change that dropped
# waypipe from home.packages altogether would leave every "does not have it"
# case passing, which is the failure mode a gate test is most likely to decay
# into.
#
#   ./tests/waypipe.sh            # tests this checkout
#   ./tests/waypipe.sh /path/to/flake
set -u

FLAKE="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)}"
[ -f "$FLAKE/flake.nix" ] || { echo "no flake.nix in: $FLAKE" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $FLAKE"

PKG=waypipe
# The two ends of the forward. Kept as a list here rather than spelled into the
# loop so the "both ends, or neither" case below can count it.
PAIR=(shiori utsuho)

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# The package names in one host's profile. `pname or name` because home.packages
# holds a mix -- nixpkgs derivations, this repo's writeShellScriptBin wrappers,
# flake inputs' packages -- and not all of them carry a pname.
#
# nix eval's stderr is noise on a healthy box and the whole story on a broken
# one, so it is held back and printed only on failure. Swallowing it would turn
# a broken checkout into a host that simply "does not have waypipe", which is a
# passing case for four of the six hosts here.
packages_for() { # packages_for <host>
  if ! nix eval --json "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.config.home.packages" \
    --apply 'ps: builtins.map (p: p.pname or p.name or "?") ps' 2>"$D/err"; then
    echo >&2; echo "nix eval failed for $1's home.packages:" >&2; cat "$D/err" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

has_pkg() { # has_pkg <host>
  packages_for "$1" | jq -e --arg p "$PKG" 'any(. == $p)' >/dev/null
}

# The store path of one host's waypipe, so the two ends can be compared. Empty
# if that host has none.
waypipe_drv() { # waypipe_drv <host>
  nix eval --raw "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.pkgs.$PKG" 2>/dev/null || true
}

check() { # check <desc> <expected: yes|no> <host>
  n=$((n + 1))
  local desc=$1 want=$2 host=$3 got=no
  has_pkg "$host" && got=yes
  if [ "$want" = "$got" ]; then
    echo "ok   $desc"
  else
    echo "FAIL $desc: expected $PKG present=$want, got present=$got"
    fails=$((fails + 1))
  fi
}

# --- the pair ----------------------------------------------------------------
# The laptop with the display and the desktop with the GPU. Each is the other's
# far end, which is why neither one alone would be worth installing.
for host in "${PAIR[@]}"; do
  check "$host (one end of the forward) has $PKG" yes "$host"
done

# --- the hosts outside it ----------------------------------------------------
# Not "cannot run it" -- waypipe would work on any of these. They are not in the
# pair, and the gate exists so the closure carries ffmpeg/vulkan/gbm only where
# something asks for it.
check "setsuna (not in the pair) does not have $PKG" no setsuna
check "fujiwara (headless, not in the pair) does not have $PKG" no fujiwara
check "kyuusaku (headless, not ours) does not have $PKG" no kyuusaku
check "mari (darwin) does not have $PKG" no mari

# --- both ends, or neither ---------------------------------------------------
# The case the pair-shaped gate exists for: half a forward is not a working
# forward, and a one-host gate is the plausible drift.
n=$((n + 1))
present=0
for host in "${PAIR[@]}"; do has_pkg "$host" && present=$((present + 1)); done
if [ "$present" -eq "${#PAIR[@]}" ] || [ "$present" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "ok   the pair is all-or-nothing ($present/${#PAIR[@]} have $PKG)"
else
  echo "FAIL only $present of ${#PAIR[@]} pair hosts have $PKG: half a forward forwards nothing"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

# --- the two ends agree ------------------------------------------------------
# waypipe rejects a wire-version mismatch outright. Same flake.lock, same
# x86_64-linux, so the two store paths must be identical; if they ever diverge
# the forward fails at connect time with a version error, not at build time.
n=$((n + 1))
a=$(waypipe_drv "${PAIR[0]}"); b=$(waypipe_drv "${PAIR[1]}")
if [ -n "$a" ] && [ "$a" = "$b" ]; then
  echo "ok   both ends are the same $PKG ($(basename "$a"))"
else
  echo "FAIL the two ends differ: ${PAIR[0]}=${a:-<none>} ${PAIR[1]}=${b:-<none>}"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

# --- the teeth ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Both directions have to be represented, or the suite passes having checked
# nothing. Without the first, waypipe removed from home.nix entirely is a green
# run; without the second, waypipe handed to every host is a green run the other
# way.
n=$((n + 1))
if has_pkg shiori; then
  echo "ok   at least one host still has $PKG (cases are not vacuous)"
else
  echo "FAIL no host has $PKG: every 'does not have it' case above is vacuous"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

n=$((n + 1))
if has_pkg mari; then
  echo "FAIL every host has $PKG: the host gate is gone, not merely wrong"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
else
  echo "ok   at least one host still lacks $PKG (the gate is doing something)"
fi

echo
if [ "$fails" -eq 0 ]; then echo "all $n passed"; else echo "$fails of $n failed"; fi
exit $((fails > 0))
EOF
chmod +x tests/waypipe.sh && echo written

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

content.content:
Merge branch 'hyprlock-pending-race'

---8<---
hyprlock: patch the race that freezes the lock screen clock

The clock on the lock screen stops a few seconds after locking and stays
stopped. Unlocking at 12:02 today showed 05:12 -- the time the screen locked --
and hyprlock had logged "Trying to update label, but a resource is still
pending! Skipping update." 29,532 times across the 6h50m in between.

Mechanism, in hyprlock 0.9.6 src/renderer/AsyncResourceManager.cpp:

  void CAsyncResourceManager::enqueue(...) {
      m_gatherer.enqueue(resource);   // first line: worker renders and emits
      ...
      resource->m_events.finished.listenStatic(...);   // last line: too late
  }

The gatherer is a single worker that wakes on enqueue, calls render() and emits
`finished` straight away. Every one of our labels runs a command that returns in
milliseconds, so the emit routinely lands before the main thread reaches
listenStatic() -- and an emit with no listener is dropped, not queued. Nothing
then schedules onResourceFinished() for that id, the widget's onAssetUpdate()
never runs, and CLabel::m_pendingResource stays true forever. Every later tick
of that label takes the early return at the top of CLabel::onTimerUpdate() and
logs the warning above.

Being a race, it bites per request rather than at startup, which is why the
clock (update:1000) and the faillock label (update:5000) both wedged on that run
while the date label (update:60000) did not, and why the two locks earlier the
same morning look clean in the journal -- both were PrepareForSleep locks that
suspended immediately, so no timer ever ran.

The patch registers the listener, and records the resource in m_resources that
onResourceFinished() looks the id up in, before handing it to the gatherer.
There is no symmetric hazard: the callback only schedules a 0ms timer, which the
main thread cannot process until it has returned from enqueue().

Upstream is hyprwm/hyprlock#1071, open, affecting 0.9.5, 0.9.6 and main; the
reorder here is the fix that report proposes. A workaround we carry needs
something that says when to stop carrying it, because a patch that has silently
become a no-op still applies and still builds -- so tests/hyprlock-pending-race.sh
reads the hyprlock source nixpkgs pins and case 1 fails the day upstream does
this itself, naming the three things to delete. The other four cases cover the
patch applying under the same `patch -p1` the build uses, both statements ending
up on the right side of the handoff, and the patch actually being listed in
pkgs.hyprlock rather than merely existing on disk.

Verified: 5/5 new cases, 35/35 hyprlock-faillock, all six host configs evaluate,
and pkgs.hyprlock builds with both patches applied.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log --oneline -1
home: install waypipe on the shiori/utsuho forwarding pair

waypipe is the Wayland answer to `ssh -X`: `waypipe ssh utsuho <app>` starts the
application on the far host and renders its surfaces here, over the ssh channel.
Nothing in the profile did this before -- pkgs.xauth and X forwarding cover X11
clients only, and a Wayland-native application over plain ssh has no display to
connect to at all.

Gated on a two-host list rather than isDesktop, because waypipe is never
installed for a host, it is installed for a *pair*. The invocation starts two
waypipes: one beside the compositor that will show the window, one beside the
application. Neither half is any use alone, which is what the gate has to encode
-- shiori (the laptop that is present) and utsuho (the amd desktop worth
reaching for) are the two ends that have a reason to forward. setsuna and mari
would run it perfectly well and have nothing to point it at, and it is not free:
this build links ffmpeg, vulkan-loader and mesa's gbm so DMABUF and `--video`
work, so the closure grows on every host the package lands on.

The pair shape is the thing worth testing, so tests/waypipe.sh asserts it rather
than mere presence. Two cases are about drift a presence check would miss: that
the pair is all-or-nothing (half a forward forwards nothing, and a gate narrowed
to one host is the plausible edit), and that the two ends resolve to the *same*
store path -- the 0.10 rewrite (C -> Rust) changed the wire format and waypipe
refuses a version mismatch rather than negotiating down, so "both have waypipe"
is not the property that makes a forward work, "both have this waypipe" is. It
holds because both hosts are x86_64-linux out of one flake.lock; the case exists
so it fails loudly if that ever stops being true. The teeth at the end are the
same two the aur-helper suite carries, for the same reason: without them,
waypipe deleted outright and waypipe given to everyone are both green runs.

One non-obvious dependency, recorded in the comment because the symptom points
at the wrong place: `waypipe ssh` resolves `waypipe` on the far end through the
non-interactive `$SHELL -c` sshd hands it, which reads .zshenv and never .zshrc
-- the same constraint the MOSH_SERVER_NETWORK_TMOUT note in zsh.nix describes.
It resolves because home-manager sources hm-session-vars.sh from .zshenv under
`if [[ ! -o login ]]`, and that file puts ~/.nix-profile/bin first on PATH
(checked in the generated .zshenv on shiori, line 1 and line 3).

Verified: 10/10 new cases, red first (2 pair cases failing on the absent
package, plus the vacuity tooth), 8/8 aur-helper unchanged, and both
shiori's and utsuho's activationPackage evaluate with waypipe-0.11.0 in the
closure. utsuho is not reachable from here to switch -- tailscale is logged out
on shiori -- so that host picks this up on its own next run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

# pi, not opencode. pi's findings channel is a generated TypeScript
# extension rather than an MCP server (pi ships no MCP client), and drovr
# writes it per review pass — see cli/src/pi_extension.rs upstream.
#
review_agent = "pi"
worktree = true
# Reviews run on gemma, pinned explicitly rather than left to pi's own
# default so this file says which model reviewed. LAST in the file because
# a TOML table swallows every key after it — the top-level settings above
# have to be emitted first.
#
# gemma returns a panel in seconds rather than minutes. That is the model
# being fast, not a reviewer skipping the diff — read the findings, not
# the wall clock. The delivery floor that used to reject exactly this is
# gone (drovr f016dcc); it could not tell "did not read" from "reads
# quickly" and so refused every review on a fast backend.
#
# glm-5.3 was tried instead and does not DELIVER: measured 2026-09-02 on
# a 278-line diff, four fresh iterations, sixteen reviewers, every one
# provably started (pi extension loaded, seed delivered), worked 8-25
# minutes, then exited without ever calling `submit_findings`. 0 of 4
# angles, four times running.
#
# Only the REVIEWER is pinned here; interactive pi takes the same gemma
# from pi.nix as its default.
[agents.pi]
command = "pi"
review_model = "google/gemma-4-31b-it"
=== angles
Spawn one review panel for `task`, wait, merge, exit 0/3/2/1.

Two forms:

```text drovr code-review run <RUN> <TASK>                    # inside a pipeline run drovr code-review run --base <rev> [--dir <repo>] <TASK>   # anywhere else ```

The second exists because `drovr:code-review` is unconditional while `drovr:using-drovr`'s escalation contract says to work INLINE until the work outgrows one context — so the agent that followed the contract correctly was the one with no run, and no way to review its change (forge#108). `--base` supplies what `<TASK>-base.sha` supplies in a run, so nothing has to have been recorded before the first edit: after the fact you know your own branch point, `git merge-base HEAD main`. `--dir` defaults to the current directory.

The panel, the brief, the resume and the merged findings are identical between the two; only the ADDRESSING changes. name: dotfiles-master-moves-under-you
description: "dotfiles master advances concurrently mid-session; re-check it before any review verdict or merge, and never merge without asking"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 208f08a9-7bb4-4404-8c5d-1ff033bc2d1b
  modified: 2026-09-30T12:02:13.944Z
---

`master` in `/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles` advanced four times during a single
session on 2026-09-28 (`f242ab9` → `2030f03` → `288c6a4` → `1df6305`), forward
each time, not amended. Something else commits to it concurrently.

**Why:** a branch based on a stale master makes `git diff master..HEAD` show the
*reverse* of master's newer commits. A review of that range reports findings
against someone else's commits (two arrived against `tests/system-packages.sh`,
which the branch never touched) and a merge off it would resurrect deleted
code — one rebase hit a real conflict where master had dropped
`warp-terminal` from the exact `home.packages` block being edited.

**How to apply:** `git rev-parse master` immediately before dispatching a
reviewer and again before merging; rebase with
`git rebase --onto master <old-base> <branch>` when it moved.

**Never derive a review base from local `master`.** It lags too. On 2026-09-30
`EnterWorktree` branched from `origin/master` (`74f80cf`) while local `master`
sat 5 commits behind at `594ae56`, so
`drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD master)"` reviewed five
other commits — `install/finalize-ssh.sh`, `mise.toml`, an elephant restart
trigger — and returned "clean" for a diff mostly nobody in this session wrote.
It reads as a pass. Take the base from the worktree's own branch point
(`git rev-parse origin/master`, or `HEAD` before the first edit), commit the
work first so the range is exactly it, and check the reviewers' `basis` names
*your* files before believing the verdict.

**Do not ask before pushing the other writer's commits.** On 2026-09-28 local
master sat 12 commits ahead of origin with another session's in-progress `wif`
work, and `hms` pushes all of it. Stopping to confirm got: "yes obviously push
everything." The concurrent writer is the same person, so their unpushed work is
theirs to ship — treat a moved master as a rebase problem, not a consent
problem, and just run `hms`. Still worth one line in the report naming what else
went out. Related: [[dotfiles-worktree-for-edits]],
[[push-implies-hms]], [[drovr-panel-flaky-angles]]

name: dont-hand-back-work-already-done
description: "Never close with a \"next action\" that repeats a command already run; close with the decision only I can make."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 6c224709-d04c-4f6c-a818-73cc775fbfe7
  modified: 2026-09-30T20:09:40.772Z
---

Do not end a report with a try-it command for something already run and reported
green. On the hyprlock clock patch (2026-09-30) the test had been run four
times, last on the committed tree, 5/5 — and the closing line was still "run
`./tests/hyprlock-pending-race.sh` yourself, then tell me to merge". Response:
"why didn't you just run the test? and yes, merge".

**Why:** the i-have-adhd close ("end with one concrete next action doable in
under two minutes") is for work that genuinely remains. Spending it on a
re-run adds a step to my queue that buys nothing, and it reads as hedging about
a result already verified. The whole point of reporting evidence is that I do
not have to go re-collect it.

**How to apply:** the closing action is the decision only I can make — merge,
`hms`, drop it — not a command re-running verification. If everything is done
and nothing needs deciding, say so and stop; no closing line is better than a
made-up one. Same reflex as [[keep-test-harnesses-in-repo]]: do the thing,
don't offer it.

content.content:
git-credential-fj = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "git-credential-fj" ''
    set -euo pipefail

    # Only `get` is ours to answer — fj owns store/erase.
    [ "''${1:-}" = "get" ] || exit 0

    host=""
    while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
      [ -n "$key" ] || break
      case "$key" in
        host) host="$value" ;;
      esac
    done
    [ -n "$host" ] || exit 0

    # fj writes keys.json to its ProjectDirs data dir: on Linux that is
    # $XDG_DATA_HOME (~/.local/share); on macOS it is ~/Library/Application
    # Support/forgejo-cli.forgejo-cli, NOT ~/.local/share — so on darwin the XDG
    # path never exists and the shim must fall back to app-support, or git drops
    # to a prompt. (fj still reads its *config*, client_ids, from ~/.config on
    # both, so only this data path is platform-split.)
    keys="''${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/forgejo-cli/keys.json"
    [ -r "$keys" ] || keys="$HOME/Library/Application Support/forgejo-cli.forgejo-cli/keys.json"
    [ -r "$keys" ] || exit 0

    # expires_at is time::OffsetDateTime's serde tuple, in order:
    # [year, day-of-year, hour, minute, second, nanos, offset-h, offset-m,
    # offset-s]. jq's mktime wants [year, month0, mday, h, m, s, wday, yday]
    # and is UTC-based, so build January 1st and add the ordinal by hand.
    # `-e` makes "still valid" exit 0; anything else — expired, absent
    # (Application login or unknown host), or unparseable — exits nonzero.
    if ! ${lib.getExe pkgs.jq} -e --arg h "$host" '
      .hosts[$h].expires_at
      | if type == "array" and length >= 9 then
          ([.[0], 0, 1, .[2], .[3], .[4], 0, 0] | mktime)
            + (.[1] - 1) * 86400
            - (.[6] * 3600 + .[7] * 60 + .[8])
          > now
        else true end
    ' "$keys" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      # Best-effort: a failed refresh still falls through to whatever is on
      # disk rather than dropping git to a terminal prompt.
      ${lib.optionalString (!isDarwin) ''${pkgs.util-linux}/bin/flock -w 60 "''${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-''${TMPDIR:-/tmp}}/git-credential-fj.lock" \''}
        ${lib.getExe pkgs.forgejo-cli} -H "$host" whoami >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    fi

    # A nonzero exit aborts git's whole operation rather than falling through
    # to a prompt, so a half-written keys.json degrades to "no credential".
    token=$(${lib.getExe pkgs.jq} -r --arg h "$host" '.hosts[$h].token // empty' "$keys" 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
    [ -n "$token" ] || exit 0

    # Forgejo ignores the basic-auth username when the password is a token.
    printf 'username=oauth2\npassword=%s\n' "$token"
  '';

  # `hms` — switch this host, but let the forge do the building.
  #
  # A local switch compiles whatever is not in attic; the in-cluster runner has
  # far more of everything and pushes its result to attic, so waiting for CI and
  # then switching turns the switch into a pure download. The wait is only worth
  # it because the closure CI pushes is bit-identical to the one we would build.
  #
  # Refuses on a dirty tree: CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch
  # is one CI can never reproduce, and silently building it locally would hide
  # that. `--local` is the escape hatch for exactly that case.
  hms = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "hms" ''
    set -euo pipefail

    # Seams, all defaulted to the real thing. tests/hms-ci-poll.sh drives the
    # built script through them: a throwaway repo, a stub forge, a stub
    # credential helper and a marker-file "switch", with the status poll bounded

---
name: hms-poll-token-expiry
description: "hms's CI poll 401s on long runs because it snapshots the OAuth token once and never refreshes it"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 76e28998-3060-4d63-bc94-0799c80d0e50
  modified: 2026-09-28T21:36:25.925Z
---

`hms` reads `.hosts["forge.ko.ag"].token` from `keys.json` **once**, into a
curlrc that lives for the whole run (`home.nix`, just below the `hms` git-push
block). The `forge.ko.ag` login is an OAuth grant whose access token expires
~1 hour out, and the CI poll loop is bounded at an hour — so any run that
outlives the token's remaining life starts 401ing mid-poll, prints
"still waiting", burns the budget and gives up without switching.

The push in the same invocation succeeds, because it goes through
`git-credential-fj`, which does the expiry check and pokes `fj whoami` to
refresh. Only the polling path lacks it.

**Why:** the 401 branch's own advice — `fj auth add-token` — is a trap. An
application token has no `expires_at` and skips the refresh poke entirely, so
it "fixes" the symptom by abandoning the OAuth login.

**How to apply:** when `hms` reports "rejected our token (HTTP 401)", do not add
an application token; re-authenticate, or fix the refresh. Note `hms`'s give-up
branch already exits 1 correctly — if you see exit 0 from a failed `hms`, check
whether you piped it (`hms | tail` reports tail's status, not hms's).
See [[push-implies-hms]].

Measured 2026-09-30: the token in `~/.local/share/forgejo-cli/keys.json` has a
**one-hour** lifetime (`iat`/`exp` an hour apart), and an expired one fails any
forge API call with `token has invalid claims: token is expired`. `fj whoami`
refreshes it in place, so run that immediately before a forge API call rather
than reusing a token read earlier in the session.

---
name: fj-refresh-token-already-used
description: "hms push dies with \"Credentials are incorrect or have expired\" when fj's OAuth refresh chain is consumed — `fj whoami` can no longer fix it, only an interactive re-login"
metadata:
  type: project
---

Measured 2026-09-30 21:40 UTC: `hms` failed at the **push**, not the poll, with
`remote: Credentials are incorrect or have expired` /
`fatal: Authentication failed for 'https://forge.ko.ag/sauyon/dotfiles.git/'`.
The stored access token had expired at 20:03:22 UTC (`expires_at` in
`~/.local/share/forgejo-cli/keys.json`), and the refresh `git-credential-fj`
pokes on that path no longer works:

    $ fj -H forge.ko.ag whoami
    Error: api error: token was already used
    Location: src/keys.rs:155:32

`refresh_token` is still present in `keys.json`, so nothing looks missing — the
grant is what is gone. Forgejo rotates refresh tokens and treats a reuse as
compromise, invalidating the chain, so once a refresh token has been spent by
something else the stored one is permanently dead.

**Why this is not [[hms-poll-token-expiry]]:** that memory records the push path
as the *working* one, because `git-credential-fj` checks `expires_at` and pokes
`fj whoami`. That is true only while the refresh chain is alive. When it is not,
both paths fail, the helper's `|| true` swallows the error, and git reports plain
bad credentials with nothing pointing at OAuth. The helper's `flock` guards two
of its *own* refreshes from racing; a bare `fj` run outside it is unguarded and
can spend the token the helper is about to use.

**How to apply:** `fj whoami` succeeding is the check, not `refresh_token` being
present. When it returns "token was already used", the fix is an interactive
re-login the agent cannot do — surface it: `fj auth login -H forge.ko.ag`.
Do **not** reach for `fj auth add-token`; per [[hms-poll-token-expiry]] an
application token has no `expires_at`, skips the refresh poke, and "fixes" this
by abandoning the OAuth login. Nothing is pushed or switched when this happens,
so the local `master` is ahead of `origin` until the re-login and a fresh `hms`.
EOF

content.content:
## Key facts

- **The cache is private.** Anonymous `GET .../nix-cache-info` returns attic's
  own `401` (not a Cloudflare challenge). Pulling therefore needs a **read-only
  token** presented via netrc — there is no anonymous read.
- **Public signing key** (safe to commit, not a secret):
  `kube:REDACTED`
- **These boxes are Arch + Determinate Nix, multi-user, with `trusted-users =
  root`.** This is the crux: nix **ignores** `substituters` /
  `trusted-public-keys` / `netrc-file` set in a *non-trusted* user's
  `~/.config/nix/nix.conf`. So the cache config must reach the **daemon**, i.e.
  live under `/etc`, not in home-manager. That is why this is wired through
  `system/deploy` (sudo → `/etc`) rather than `home.nix`.

## How it is wired (Linux: utsuho, setsuna, fujiwara, shiori)

Three pieces, all applied by `./system/deploy` (sudo):

1. `system/etc/nix/nix.custom.conf` → `/etc/nix/nix.custom.conf`
   Determinate `!include`s this from `/etc/nix/nix.conf`. Adds the substituter
   and trusted key with the **`extra-`** forms (append, don't replace — keeps
   `cache.nixos.org` and FlakeHub).

2. `system/etc/determinate/config.json` → `/etc/determinate/config.json`
   ```json
   { "authentication": { "additionalNetrcSources": ["/etc/determinate/netrc.custom"] } }
   ```
   This is the Determinate-supported hook for extra netrc entries. Determinate
   **merges** the referenced file into its synthesized `/nix/var/determinate/netrc`.

   > Gotcha: do **not** append to `/nix/var/determinate/netrc` directly — that
   > file is regenerated by `determinate-nixd` (e.g. on boot) and your line is
   > lost. `additionalNetrcSources` survives regeneration. And you cannot

Running. Meanwhile, three things worth your attention:

1. **Your waypipe change is in `origin/master`** — `e22c617` is an ancestor of the pushed `50954f3`, CI run 126 green. utsuho gets it on its next `hms`.
2. **`master` moved under me**: `50954f3 wire shiori -> utsuho over the Kon WireGuard overlay` (14:44, yours) landed on top of my merge and went out with this push. No conflict — it touches `system/deploy` and `system/packages.*`, not the `home.packages` block. It isn't deployed here yet; no wg interface is up on shiori.
3. **attic's NAR delivery is broken from shiori, independent of this work.** `https://attic.ko.ag/kube/nix-cache-info` answers (401, as documented), but `.../nar/<hash>.nar` returns 307 to a target nix can't connect to — every attempt, 4 retries each. That defeats the whole point of `hms`: the switch stops being a download. Not caused by the WireGuard commit (no interface, normal routes); my guess is the redirect target is only reachable on the tailnet, and tailscale is logged out here — but I can't see the `Location` without the read token, so that's a hypothesis, not a finding.

content.text:
Nothing to restore — you're online via the `orie` hotspot, no WireGuard interface up, `cache.nixos.org` answers HTTP 200 in 0.5s. And `connection.autoconnect: no`, so it won't come back on its own.

**Why it killed the network.** The `Kon-WireGuard` NM profile is a **full tunnel** pointed at a peer that isn't working:

```
wireguard.peers:      ... allowed-ips=0.0.0.0/0;::/0 endpoint=<home public IP>:51820
ipv4.never-default:   no          # so NM installs the default route INTO the tunnel
ipv4.dns:             10.9.0.1    # resolver only reachable INSIDE the tunnel
ipv4.addresses:       10.9.0.2/32
```

A WireGuard link reports `UP,LOWER_UP` whether or not a handshake ever completed — that's why I saw it up one minute and gone the next. So activating it moves *all* v4+v6 traffic and DNS into a tunnel that isn't carrying packets. Total blackout, including name resolution, which is exactly what you saw.

**The fix is to make it a split tunnel**, which is also all you actually need: the point is reaching utsuho at `10.9.0.6`, not routing your internet through home.

```
nmcli con mod Kon-WireGuard \
  wireguard.peers '<pubkey> allowed-ips=10.9.0.0/24 endpoint=<home ip>:51820' \
  ipv4.never-default yes ipv6.never-default yes ipv4.dns ''
```

That keeps your default route on wifi and sends only `10.9.0.0/24` down the tunnel. If it still can't reach `10.9.0.6` afterward, the remaining suspect is the UCG side — shiori's public key not registered as a peer, or `51820` not open — not your routing.

On 2026-10-02 activating the `Kon-WireGuard` NetworkManager profile on shiori
took the whole network down, DNS included. The profile was a **full tunnel**:
`allowed-ips=0.0.0.0/0;::/0`, `ipv4.never-default no`,
`wireguard.ip4-auto-default-route` at auto (`-1`), and `ipv4.dns 10.9.0.1`. With
`0.0.0.0/0` in allowed-ips NM turns on its auto-default-route policy routing, so
every packet *and* the resolver moved into a tunnel that was not carrying
traffic. A wg link reports `UP,LOWER_UP` with or without a handshake, so it looks
connected while nothing works.

Fixed on-host, not in the repo (`nmcli con mod Kon-WireGuard`):
`wireguard.ip4-auto-default-route no`, `wireguard.ip6-auto-default-route no`,
`ipv4.never-default yes`, `ipv6.never-default yes`, `ipv4.dns ""`,
`ipv4.routes 10.9.0.0/24`. Default route then stays on wifi, only the overlay
subnet goes down the tunnel, and that is all the waypipe pair needs — the point
is reaching utsuho at 10.9.0.6, not routing internet through home.

**Why the tunnel still does not come up** (measured the same day, after the fix):
`ip -s link show Kon-WireGuard` shows TX 148 bytes / 1 packet and RX 0 — one
WireGuard handshake initiation, never answered. Not a routing problem. The home
gateway is alive and its IP current (TCP 443 open at the endpoint; ICMP filtered,
which is normal for the UCG), and outbound UDP from the phone hotspot works (a
UDP DNS query to 1.1.1.1 got a reply). So the silence is UCG-side: shiori's
public key not in the WG server's peer list, or 51820 not forwarded. WireGuard is
deliberately silent for both, so they cannot be told apart from the client.

**How to apply:** `ip -s link show <wgdev>` is the first check on any dead
WireGuard — TX>0 with RX=0 means the peer is not answering, and no amount of
local routing work will change it. Never leave `allowed-ips=0.0.0.0/0` on a
profile that only needs one subnet. Note the repo's own mechanism for this link
is `wg-quick@wg0` + `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf` via `./system/deploy` (commit
50954f3), which is NOT deployed on shiori — the NM profile is a second,
hand-made path to the same place, and `AllowedIPs` in a future `wg0.conf` needs
the same `10.9.0.0/24` narrowing. Related: [[orie-exit-node-blocks-lan]].
EOF

content.text:
Done — profile is split-tunnelled and persistent, and you stayed online the whole time.

**It's down because the peer never answers.** Not routing:

```
TX: 148 bytes / 1 packet   ← one WG handshake init, sent
RX:   0 bytes / 0 packets   ← nothing, ever
```

I ruled out everything on this side:
1. **Home gateway is alive, IP is current** — TCP 443 open at the endpoint (ICMP filtered, normal for a UCG). So the endpoint isn't stale.
2. **Outbound UDP works from the hotspot** — a raw UDP DNS query to `1.1.1.1:53` came back with 61 bytes.
3. **Routing is now correct** — `ip route get 10.9.0.6` → `dev Kon-WireGuard src 10.9.0.2`, default route still on wifi.

That leaves the UCG side: either **shiori's public key isn't in the WireGuard peer list**, or **51820 isn't forwarded to the WG server**. WireGuard answers unknown keys and closed ports identically — with silence — so those two can't be separated from here by design. (The one thing I can't fully exclude: the carrier blocking UDP *specifically* on 51820 while allowing 53.)

Your next move, ~2 minutes:

```
! sudo wg show Kon-WireGuard public-key
```

Then check that string against the client list in the UCG's WireGuard config. If it's missing, that's the whole bug.

**Two notes:**
- I left the tunnel up. It's harmless now (no default route, internet verified at start and end) and it'll start working the moment the UCG side is fixed. `autoconnect` is still `no`, so a reboot won't bring it back on its own.
- This fix lives only in the NM profile on this host. The repo's mechanism (`wg-quick@wg0` + `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf`, commit `50954f3`) is still not deployed here — and if you go that route, that conf needs `AllowedIPs = 10.9.0.0/24`, not `0.0.0.0/0`, or you'll reproduce today's outage.

Still unverified: **waypipe on utsuho**. It's in `origin/master` and CI was green, but I've had no path to the box, so I haven't seen the binary.

Yes — and that means one half of what I told you was wrong. If the peer *is* the gateway, WireGuard terminates **on** the UCG, so there's nothing to "forward to a WG server" — 51820 is a service on the router itself. Scratch that line; it points you at the wrong screen.

Corrected candidate list, and it's shorter:
1. shiori's public key isn't in the UCG's WireGuard client list (or that client was regenerated/deleted).
2. The WireGuard VPN server on the UCG is toggled off, or listening on a port other than 51820.

content.text:
Found something better than a guess. All three downloaded client configs agree on the server's identity, and the NM profile matches them:

| Field | Downloaded configs | NM profile |
|---|---|---|
| Peer public key | `/REDACTED` | same ✓ |
| Endpoint | `<home IP>:51820` | same ✓ |
| Client address | `10.9.0.6` (utsuho), `10.9.0.5` (Client-4, kakugyouki) | **`10.9.0.2`** ✗ |

So the router's key and port are right — but the profile's address, `10.9.0.2`, matches **none** of the clients the UCG generated. That reads as a hand-rolled profile: correct server details copied in, paired with a locally-generated private key the UCG has never been told about. A WireGuard server ignores an unknown key in exactly the silence we're seeing.

I can't prove it from here — shiori could be a registered client whose config was never downloaded to this box. The one-line check is `sudo wg show Kon-WireGuard public-key` against the UCG's client list.

Also confirmed: `Kon-WireGuard-utsuho.conf` has `Address = 10.9.0.6`, which matches the repo commit, so utsuho is genuinely a registered client at that address.

New client is `10.9.0.2` — same address the hand-rolled profile claimed, which is consistent with that key never having been registered. Importing now.

One thing: `nmcli con import` activates immediately, and the file is full-tunnel as Unifi ships it, so there may be a 1–2 second blackout before I harden it. The script doesn't need the network to recover from that.

CONF=/home/sauyon/downloads/Kon-WireGuard-shiori.conf
NAME=Kon-WireGuard-shiori

nmcli con import type wireguard file "$CONF" 2>&1 | tail -2
# Down it at once: as shipped it is full-tunnel and would hijack the default route.
nmcli con down "$NAME" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

nmcli con mod "$NAME" \
  wireguard.ip4-auto-default-route no \
  wireguard.ip6-auto-default-route no \
  ipv4.never-default yes \
  ipv6.never-default yes \

nmcli -g wireguard.ip4-auto-default-route,ipv4.never-default,ipv4.dns,ipv4.routes,connection.autoconnect con show "$NAME"

echo "=== up"
nmcli con up "$NAME" 2>&1 | tail -1

net_ok() { timeout 8 curl -sS -o /dev/null https://cache.nixos.org/nix-cache-info 2>/dev/null; }
if ! net_ok; then
  echo "INTERNET BROKEN — downing $NAME"; nmcli con down "$NAME" | tail -1

echo "=== counters (RX>0 means the handshake completed)"; ip -s link show "$dev" 2>/dev/null | tail -4

content.text:
Three bugs down, one decision left for you.

**Fixed:**
1. **Full tunnel → blackout.** Split-tunnelled: `ipv4.routes 10.9.0.0/24`, `never-default yes`, auto-default-route off, tunnel DNS cleared. Internet verified before, during and after every step.
2. **Unregistered key.** New `Kon-shiori` profile imported from your download (via a short-named copy — NM caps the derived interface name at 15 chars, and `Kon-WireGuard-shiori` is 20). Handshake completes: RX 476 B, ping `10.9.0.6` 0% loss.
3. **MTU.** NM used the stock 1420; the real path ceiling is 1368. That's why ping was clean and TCP 22 opened but ssh hung — key exchange is the first packet big enough to black-hole. Set `wireguard.mtu 1368`; ssh now reaches a real answer.

**Your call — utsuho's host key is unknown.** Not a mismatch: there's no `known_hosts` entry for `utsuho` or `10.9.0.6` at all, and no `cert-authority` lines, so this is first contact with nothing to compare against. utsuho offers:

```
ssh-ed25519 SHA256:REDACTED
```

Confirm it out-of-band, on utsuho itself:

```
ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
```

If it matches, tell me and I'll add it to `known_hosts`, then finish the waypipe check in the same breath. I'm not writing an unverified host key in on your behalf.

One note on the MTU: 1368 is a property of the hotspot path. On a network with a smaller path MTU the same ssh hang returns — say the word and I'll drop it to 1280, which works everywhere for a little throughput.

content.text:
Host key is sorted. The remaining wall is authorization, and it needs a hand on utsuho — I have no way in.

**State:** tunnel up, MTU right, host key trusted, sshd reached. utsuho answers `Permission denied (publickey,password)`. shiori offers exactly one key, `SHA256:REDACTED`, and utsuho doesn't accept it.

**Your move, ~1 minute on utsuho:**

```
echo 'ssh-ed25519 REDACTED sauyon@shiori' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
```

Then say the word and I'll finish the waypipe verification.

**One thing worth a decision first, not just a reflex append:** `ssh-tpm-agent` is running on shiori and reachable, but **holds no identities**. If the fleet's intended path is the TPM-backed key with authorized keys published through `ssh-oidc`, then pasting a plain on-disk key into `authorized_keys` works around that machinery rather than fixing it — and utsuho is an Arch box, so the repo's nixos/darwin `ssh-oidc` modules don't cover it anyway. Appending the key is fine as a deliberate choice; I'd just rather you make it than have me quietly pick the easy path.

content.text:
No — plain software key. That also corrects what I said last message.

```
id_ed25519        -> -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----   (399 bytes)
~/.ssh/*.tpm      -> none
ssh-tpm-agent     -> running, 0 identities
```

A TPM-backed key would be `BEGIN TSS2 PRIVATE KEY`. This isn't one, and there are no TPM-format ssh keys on the box at all — which is also why the agent is empty: it's running with nothing to load, not failing to load something.

So my caveat was wrong. You wouldn't be working around TPM/OIDC machinery by appending that key, because no ssh-side TPM path exists here. The repo's TPM usage is the **WIF device identity** (`wifTpmHosts = [ "shiori" "fujiwara" ]`, `install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh`) for sops/GCP STS — a different key for a different job. And `ssh-oidc` is wired in `flake.nix` for the darwin/nixos modules, nothing in `home.nix` touches shiori or utsuho.

A TPM-backed ssh key would be new work (`ssh-tpm-keygen`, then authorize *that* pubkey), not a restoration of something broken.

So the step stands, with no asterisk — on utsuho:

```
echo 'ssh-ed25519 REDACTED sauyon@shiori' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
```

Then I'll finish the waypipe check.

content.text:
Swapped. shiori now has a TPM-sealed key and offers nothing else.

**What changed:**
1. **New key**: `~/.ssh/id_ecdsa.tpm` (`BEGIN TSS2 PRIVATE KEY`, 0600) — ECDSA P-256, the strongest your TPM supports for ssh (it offers ecdsa 256/384 and rsa 2048; no ed25519, that's a TPM 2.0 limitation, not a config choice).
2. **In the agent, and it survives reboot** — restarted `ssh-tpm-agent` and the key re-appeared on its own, so no `ssh-tpm-add` at every login.
3. **Old key backed up**: `~/.ssh/backup/id_ed25519` (dir 700, key 600). Out of ssh's default search path, so it's never offered — `ssh -v` now shows exactly one key offered, the TPM one.

**Your step on utsuho:**

```
echo 'ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 REDACTED/2sHcNvjK2IeTqKXpvR/REDACTED/xGcGkcGpg+0= sauyon@shiori (tpm)' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
```

**Three things to know:**
- **Any other host that trusted the old key now rejects shiori** until it gets this one. The escape valve is `ssh -i ~/.ssh/backup/id_ed25519 <host>` — that still works, it's just not automatic. Nothing local broke: shiori's own `authorized_keys` holds a `sauyon@kujira` key, not this one.
- **No passphrase.** The TPM already prevents the private key leaving the chip, which is the main thing a passphrase buys for a file-based key; adding one would mean a prompt per use. Say so and I'll set one with `ssh-tpm-keygen -p`.
- **No repo change needed** — nothing in `home.nix` or `~/.ssh/config` names `id_ed25519`; `programs.ssh-tpm-agent.enable = true` was already there, which is why the agent was running and empty.

Installed and verified on both hosts.

```
utsuho: /nix/store/8bh0c0yx0rclaq8331qsi1la536dq59y-waypipe-0.11.0/bin/waypipe

```

Identical store path on both ends — which is the property `tests/waypipe.sh` asserts at eval time, now confirmed against the real binaries. That matters because waypipe refuses a wire-version mismatch rather than negotiating down.

It also closes the one claim in my commit message I couldn't check at the time: `command -v waypipe` resolved over a **non-interactive** `ssh utsuho '<cmd>'`, which is exactly the `$SHELL -c` → `.zshenv` path `waypipe ssh` depends on. So far-end resolution works, not just the install.

**Everything from the original ask is done:**
1. `home.nix` — waypipe gated to the shiori/utsuho pair; in `origin/master`, CI green.
2. `tests/waypipe.sh` — 10/10, two clean review rounds, listed in README.
3. Both hosts switched and verified.

**Untested, and it's the one thing left:** an actual forward. `waypipe ssh utsuho <app>` will open a window on your display, so I'd rather you say go than surprise you with it. If utsuho has anything trivially graphical, that's the 30-second proof.

Incidental from the detour: the tunnel's MTU is pinned to 1368, which I measured on the `orie` hotspot. It'll keep working at home; if you ever land on a network with a smaller path MTU, ssh will hang the same way it did today and `wireguard.mtu 1280` is the bulletproof setting.

Correction to what I said a moment ago: my "the shell stripped it" probe was invalid. The `;` in that command string ended waypipe's argument list, so those `echo`s ran as *siblings* of `waypipe server`, never as its children — of course they saw no `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`. content.text: Not ghostty-specific — `pwvucontrol` fails the same way (`Failed to initialize GTK`). So GTK can't complete a Wayland connection over the forward. Prime suspect is DMABUF/GPU negotiation across two different GPUs (shiori Intel Xe3 → utsuho AMD); waypipe has `--no-gpu` for exactly that.

content.text:
Working. An app on utsuho, window on shiori:

```
class: com.saivert.pwvucontrol
title: Pipewire Volume Control
```

**Why it "didn't do anything": DMABUF.** Your command was almost certainly right — waypipe's transport was never the problem. Both halves connected, the far-end socket was created, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` was set correctly. What failed is GPU buffer sharing:

- The debug log shows `Connected waypipe-server may use dmabufs: true`, and waypipe proxying `zwp_linux_dmabuf_v1` and `wp_linux_drm_syncobj_manager_v1`.
- shiori is Intel Xe3, utsuho is AMD. The far end has to import buffers in modifiers the local GPU advertises; cross-vendor that fails, GTK can't create a surface, and you get `Failed to initialize GTK` — or, from ghostty, the bare `Gtk: Failed to open display`. No window, no useful error. Exactly "didn't do anything".
- `--no-gpu` drops to shared-memory transfer and it works first try.

**Use this now:**

```
waypipe --no-gpu ssh utsuho ghostty
```

Also worth knowing: `--video` won't rescue the GPU path — it needs the same GPU interop. Over this link shared-memory is the realistic mode; it costs CPU and bandwidth, which on a WireGuard-over-hotspot path you'll notice more than the pixel copies.

**Your call:** want me to make `--no-gpu` the default so plain `waypipe ssh utsuho …` just works? It'd be a small `home.nix` wrapper on the two pair hosts, with a test and a review round, then an `hms` cycle — call it 20 minutes. The alternative is leaving the flag explicit, which keeps the GPU path available if you ever forward between two same-vendor machines.

I'd bake it in: the flag is unmemorable, and the failure it prevents is silent.

hookInfos.command: sh -c 'if ! command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then exit 0; fi; exec entire hooks claude-code stop'

Stop — that would not have worked, and it's worth saying before I write it. `nixGLIntel` sets **no Vulkan variables at all**:

```
GBM_BACKENDS_PATH, LIBGL_DRIVERS_PATH, LIBVA_DRIVERS_PATH,
__EGL_VENDOR_LIBRARY_FILENAMES, LD_LIBRARY_PATH   ← all GL/EGL/VA-API
```

No `VK_ICD_FILENAMES`, no `VK_DRIVER_FILES`. So nixGL-wrapping waypipe — the fix I was about to apply on the strength of the `cumora` precedent — would have changed nothing. The precedent is for OpenGL; waypipe's failure is Vulkan. Checking what can actually supply an ICD:

content.text: Following the repo's existing pattern (`steam-env.sh` resolves via `drvPath` + `nix-store --realise`). Adding the RED cases:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='tests/waypipe.sh'
s=open(p).read()
marker = "# --- the teeth ---------------------------------------------------------------"
assert s.count(marker)==1

new = '''# --- the Vulkan ICD (the GPU path) -------------------------------------------
# waypipe 0.10+ rewrote DMABUF handling onto Vulkan (src/dmabuf.rs), so the
# `dmabuf: true` the binary advertises is only half the story: it also needs a
# Vulkan *driver* at runtime, and a nix-built loader on a non-NixOS host does not
# get one. The host's own manifest does not save it -- Arch's
# /usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/radeon_icd.json names the bare soname
# `libvulkan_radeon.so`, which a store-built waypipe has no path to resolve, so
# the loader finds a manifest and still comes up empty:
#
#   ERR waypipe-server src/dmabuf.rs:970:
#       Failed to create Vulkan instance: Unable to find a Vulkan driver
#
# That error is reported to the client, which drops the dmabuf protocols, and the
# far-end app then fails in GTK with "Failed to initialize GTK" or the even less
# helpful "Gtk: Failed to open display" -- no window, nothing naming Vulkan.
# `--no-gpu` papers over it by forcing shared memory. These cases are about the
# wrapper that fixes it instead, because the symptom points nowhere near the cause.
drv_for() { # drv_for <host>
  nix eval --raw "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.config.home.packages" \\
    --apply 'ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: (p.pname or "") == "waypipe") ps)).drvPath' 2>"$D/err"
}

n=$((n + 1))
if drv=$(drv_for shiori) && store=$(nix-store --realise "$drv" 2>>"$D/err" | tail -1) && [ -n "$store" ]; then
  echo "ok   waypipe realises for shiori ($(basename "$store"))"
  BIN="$store/bin/waypipe"
else
  echo "FAIL could not realise shiori's waypipe:"; cat "$D/err" >&2
  fails=$((fails + 1)); BIN=""
fi

# The wrapper has to be a wrapper. Before this change $out/bin/waypipe is the
# bare ELF and every assertion below is about a string that is simply absent.
n=$((n + 1))
icd_value=""
if [ -n "$BIN" ] && icd_value=$(grep -oE 'VK_ICD_FILENAMES[=" ]+[^"]*' "$BIN" 2>/dev/null | head -1 | sed 's/^VK_ICD_FILENAMES[=" ]*//'); then
  if [ -n "$icd_value" ]; then
    echo "ok   waypipe is wrapped and sets VK_ICD_FILENAMES"
  else
    echo "FAIL waypipe sets no VK_ICD_FILENAMES: the Vulkan/DMABUF path cannot initialise"
    fails=$((fails + 1))
  fi
else
  echo "FAIL waypipe sets no VK_ICD_FILENAMES: the Vulkan/DMABUF path cannot initialise"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

# Every manifest named must exist. A path that 404s is the failure mode a string
# match cannot see: the var is set, the loader reads nothing, and the error is
# byte-identical to having no wrapper at all.
n=$((n + 1))
if [ -n "$icd_value" ]; then
  missing=""
  IFS=':' read -r -a icds <<< "$icd_value"
  for f in "${icds[@]}"; do
    case "$f" in /nix/store/*) [ -r "$f" ] || missing="$missing $f" ;; esac
  done
  if [ -z "$missing" ]; then
    echo "ok   every store ICD manifest named exists (${#icds[@]} entries)"
  else
    echo "FAIL ICD manifests named but absent:$missing"
    fails=$((fails + 1))
  fi
else
  echo "FAIL no ICD list to check"; fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

# Both GPUs of the pair, from ONE derivation. shiori is Intel (anv) and utsuho is
# AMD (radv), and the two ends must stay the same store path -- see the case
# above -- so the wrapper cannot be keyed on the host's gpu attr. Listing both is
# what lets one package serve both ends; the loader skips an ICD whose device is
# not present.
for want in intel_icd radeon_icd; do
  n=$((n + 1))
  case "$icd_value" in
    *"$want"*) echo "ok   ICD list covers $want" ;;
    *) echo "FAIL ICD list does not cover $want: one end of the pair has no driver"
       fails=$((fails + 1)) ;;
  esac
done

# The wrap must not have cost us the feature it exists to serve.
n=$((n + 1))
if [ -n "$BIN" ] && "$BIN" --version 2>/dev/null | grep -q "dmabuf: true"; then
  echo "ok   wrapped waypipe still reports dmabuf: true"
else
  echo "FAIL wrapped waypipe does not report dmabuf: true"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

'''
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(marker, new + marker))
print("ok")
PY
bash -n tests/waypipe.sh && echo "syntax ok"

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='home.nix'
s=open(p).read()

# 1. the let binding, before hms
anchor = "  hms = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin \"hms\" ''"
assert s.count(anchor) == 1
binding = '''  # waypipe, wrapped so its DMABUF path can actually find a GPU.
  #
  # waypipe 0.10 rewrote DMABUF handling onto Vulkan (src/dmabuf.rs), so the
  # `dmabuf: true` the binary advertises is a build-time fact, not a runtime one:
  # it also needs a Vulkan driver, and a store-built loader on an Arch box has no
  # way to find one. The host's own manifest is not a fallback -- Arch's
  # /usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/radeon_icd.json names the bare soname
  # `libvulkan_radeon.so`, which a nix binary cannot resolve, so the loader reads
  # a manifest and still reports none. Measured on utsuho 2026-10-02:
  #
  #   ERR waypipe-server src/dmabuf.rs:970:
  #       Failed to create Vulkan instance: Unable to find a Vulkan driver
  #
  # waypipe then tells the client to drop the dmabuf protocols and the far-end
  # application dies in GTK init -- "Failed to initialize GTK", or from ghostty
  # the even blanker "Gtk: Failed to open display". No window and nothing naming
  # Vulkan, which is why this is worth a comment rather than a one-liner.
  #
  # Why not nixGL, the wrapper this repo already reaches for: nixGLIntel sets
  # GBM_BACKENDS_PATH, LIBGL_DRIVERS_PATH, LIBVA_DRIVERS_PATH,
  # __EGL_VENDOR_LIBRARY_FILENAMES and LD_LIBRARY_PATH -- and no Vulkan variable
  # at all. It would have changed nothing here. nixgl's separate nixVulkanIntel
  # does set VK_ICD_FILENAMES, but it also overwrites LD_LIBRARY_PATH (warning on
  # stderr as it goes) and drags in validation layers, for one variable we can set
  # ourselves.
  #
  # Both manifests, from one derivation, named rather than globbed:
  #   - Both, because shiori is Intel (anv) and utsuho AMD (radv), and the loader
  #     skips an ICD whose device is absent. Keying this on `gpu` would give the
  #     two ends different store paths, and waypipe refuses a version mismatch --
  #     see ../tests/waypipe.sh, which asserts the two ends are byte-identical.
  #   - Named, because `builtins.readDir "${pkgs.mesa}/share/..."` is
  #     import-from-derivation, and CI evaluates every host without building.
  #     A filename that moves upstream therefore fails a test, not an eval.
  # --prefix, not --set: the host's own manifests stay behind ours, so a box that
  # grows a working system ICD is not cut off from it.
  waypipe = pkgs.waypipe.overrideAttrs (old: {
    nativeBuildInputs = (old.nativeBuildInputs or [ ]) ++ [ pkgs.makeWrapper ];
    postFixup = (old.postFixup or "") + ''
      wrapProgram $out/bin/waypipe \\
        --prefix VK_ICD_FILENAMES : "${
          lib.concatStringsSep ":" [
            "${pkgs.mesa}/share/vulkan/icd.d/intel_icd.x86_64.json"
            "${pkgs.mesa}/share/vulkan/icd.d/radeon_icd.x86_64.json"
          ]
        }"
    '';
  });

'''
s = s.replace(anchor, binding + anchor)

# 2. point the package list at the wrapper
old_ref = "  ++ lib.optionals (builtins.elem hostname [ \"shiori\" \"utsuho\" ]) [\n    pkgs.waypipe\n  ]"
assert s.count(old_ref) == 1, s.count(old_ref)
new_ref = "  ++ lib.optionals (builtins.elem hostname [ \"shiori\" \"utsuho\" ]) [\n    # The nixGL-less Vulkan wrap, defined up top; pkgs.waypipe bare cannot do GPU\n    # transfers on these hosts.\n    waypipe\n  ]"
s = s.replace(old_ref, new_ref)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("patched")
PY

content.text: The wrapper is correct — makeWrapper split my colon-joined value into two `--prefix` ops, so the final value is `intel:radeon`. My *test* was wrong: the regex matched a bash-expansion line with no paths in it. Fixing both that and the "same store path" case, which was checking `pkgs.waypipe` rather than what's actually installed:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='tests/waypipe.sh'
s=open(p).read()

# --- 1. the "two ends agree" case must look at the INSTALLED derivation -------
old_drv = '''# The store path of one host's waypipe, so the two ends can be compared. Empty
# if that host has none.
waypipe_drv() { # waypipe_drv <host>
  nix eval --raw "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.pkgs.$PKG" 2>/dev/null || true
}'''
new_drv = '''# The .drv of the waypipe actually in one host's profile, so the two ends can be
# compared. Empty if that host has none.
#
# Deliberately NOT `homeConfigurations.$1.pkgs.waypipe`: that is the bare nixpkgs
# package, which is identical across hosts no matter what the profile installs, so
# a wrap applied to one end only would still have compared equal. What has to
# match is what each end will actually exec.
waypipe_drv() { # waypipe_drv <host>
  nix eval --raw "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.config.home.packages" \\
    --apply 'ps: let m = builtins.filter (p: (p.pname or "") == "waypipe") ps;
                 in if m == [ ] then "" else (builtins.head m).drvPath' 2>/dev/null || true
}'''
assert s.count(old_drv) == 1
s = s.replace(old_drv, new_drv)

old_msg = '''  echo "ok   both ends are the same $PKG ($(basename "$a"))"'''
new_msg = '''  echo "ok   both ends build the same $PKG ($(basename "$a"))"'''
assert s.count(old_msg) == 1
s = s.replace(old_msg, new_msg)

# --- 2. read the ICD list by RUNNING the wrapper, not by regex ----------------
old_extract = '''n=$((n + 1))
icd_value=""
if [ -n "$BIN" ] && icd_value=$(grep -oE 'VK_ICD_FILENAMES[=" ]+[^"]*' "$BIN" 2>/dev/null | head -1 | sed 's/^VK_ICD_FILENAMES[=" ]*//'); then
  if [ -n "$icd_value" ]; then
    echo "ok   waypipe is wrapped and sets VK_ICD_FILENAMES"
  else
    echo "FAIL waypipe sets no VK_ICD_FILENAMES: the Vulkan/DMABUF path cannot initialise"
    fails=$((fails + 1))
  fi
else
  echo "FAIL waypipe sets no VK_ICD_FILENAMES: the Vulkan/DMABUF path cannot initialise"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi'''
new_extract = '''# Read the value the wrapper really produces, by running the wrapper with its
# final `exec` rewritten into a printenv. Everything above that line -- the
# prefix arithmetic makeWrapper emits, which is five lines of bash parameter
# expansion per entry -- runs verbatim, so this tests the resulting value
# including order and de-duplication. A regex over the script does not: the
# emitted code mentions VK_ICD_FILENAMES on lines that contain no path at all,
# and an earlier version of this test matched one of those and passed vacuously.
icd_value=""
n=$((n + 1))
if [ -n "$BIN" ]; then
  icd_value=$(sed 's#^exec .*#printenv VK_ICD_FILENAMES#' "$BIN" \\
    | env -u VK_ICD_FILENAMES bash 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
fi
if [ -n "$icd_value" ]; then
  echo "ok   wrapper exports VK_ICD_FILENAMES when the environment had none"
else
  echo "FAIL wrapper exports no VK_ICD_FILENAMES: the Vulkan/DMABUF path cannot initialise"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi'''
assert s.count(old_extract) == 1
s = s.replace(old_extract, new_extract)

# --- 3. and check it PREFIXES rather than replaces ----------------------------
teeth = "# --- the teeth ---------------------------------------------------------------"
assert s.count(teeth) == 1
prefix_case = '''# --prefix, not --set: a host that grows a working system ICD must keep it. The
# store entries have to come first, though, or the broken host manifest is what
# the loader tries first.
n=$((n + 1))
if [ -n "$BIN" ]; then
  combined=$(sed 's#^exec .*#printenv VK_ICD_FILENAMES#' "$BIN" \\
    | VK_ICD_FILENAMES=/sentinel/host_icd.json bash 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
  case "$combined" in
    /nix/store/*:*/sentinel/host_icd.json) echo "ok   pre-set VK_ICD_FILENAMES is kept, after ours" ;;
    *"/sentinel/host_icd.json") echo "FAIL ours do not come first: $combined"; fails=$((fails + 1)) ;;
    *) echo "FAIL a pre-set VK_ICD_FILENAMES was discarded: $combined"; fails=$((fails + 1)) ;;
  esac
else
  echo "FAIL no wrapper to check prefix behaviour"; fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

'''
s = s.replace(teeth, prefix_case + teeth)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PY
bash -n tests/waypipe.sh && echo "syntax ok" && ./tests/waypipe.sh 2>&1 | tail -20

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log --oneline -1
home: give waypipe a Vulkan ICD, or its DMABUF path finds no GPU

`waypipe ssh utsuho <app>` opened no window and said nothing useful. ghostty
printed "Gtk: Failed to open display"; pwvucontrol got as far as "Failed to
initialize GTK". Both look like a missing display, and the display was fine --
waypipe's transport worked throughout, the far-end socket was created, and
WAYLAND_DISPLAY was set correctly in the child. With --debug the server says what
is actually wrong:

  ERR waypipe-server src/dmabuf.rs:970:
      Failed to create Vulkan instance: Unable to find a Vulkan driver

waypipe 0.10 rewrote DMABUF handling onto Vulkan, so `dmabuf: true` in
`waypipe --version` is a build-time fact: the binary also needs a Vulkan driver at
runtime, and a store-built loader on an Arch box has no way to find one. The
host's own manifest is not the fallback it looks like -- utsuho's
/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/radeon_icd.json names the bare soname
`libvulkan_radeon.so`, which a nix binary cannot resolve, so the loader reads a
manifest and still reports no driver. XDG_DATA_DIRS already includes /usr/share
over a non-interactive ssh, so the search path was never the problem.

waypipe then tells the client to drop the dmabuf protocols and the application
dies in GTK init, which is why nothing in the symptom points at Vulkan. `--no-gpu`
makes it work by forcing shared memory; this is the fix instead.

Not nixGL, even though that is the wrapper this repo already reaches for and
cumora sits behind it for a neighbouring reason: nixGLIntel sets
GBM_BACKENDS_PATH, LIBGL_DRIVERS_PATH, LIBVA_DRIVERS_PATH,
__EGL_VENDOR_LIBRARY_FILENAMES and LD_LIBRARY_PATH, and no Vulkan variable at
all -- it would have changed nothing. nixgl's separate nixVulkanIntel does set
VK_ICD_FILENAMES (and, despite the name, lists radeon_icd too), but it also
overwrites LD_LIBRARY_PATH and pulls in validation layers for one variable we can
set ourselves, so this wraps with makeWrapper directly.

Both manifests from one derivation, named rather than globbed: shiori is Intel
(anv) and utsuho AMD (radv) and the loader skips an ICD whose device is absent,
while keying the wrap on `gpu` would give the two ends different store paths --
which waypipe rejects outright. `readDir` over mesa's icd.d would be
import-from-derivation, and CI evaluates every host without building, so a
filename that moves upstream has to fail a test rather than an eval. --prefix
rather than --set, so a host that grows a working system ICD keeps it, behind ours.

tests/waypipe.sh grows from 10 cases to 17. Two of the new ones are about this
test's own failure modes rather than the code's: it reads VK_ICD_FILENAMES by
running the wrapper with its final `exec` rewritten to a printenv, because the
first version matched the variable's name with a regex and passed against one of
the five bash-expansion lines makeWrapper emits that contain no path at all; and
the "both ends are the same waypipe" case now resolves the drv from
`config.home.packages` instead of `pkgs.waypipe`, which is identical on every host
no matter what the profile installs and so would have compared equal with the wrap
on one end only.

Verified: 17/17, red first on the four ICD cases against the unwrapped ELF; and a
real forward of pwvucontrol from utsuho onto shiori's compositor with the built
wrapper as client, no --no-gpu and no VK_ICD_FILENAMES in the environment --
window present in `hyprctl clients`, zero "Unable to find a Vulkan driver", 593
dmabuf lines in the debug log, so the GPU path is in use rather than quietly
falling back. The far end used an equivalent one-line wrapper via --remote-bin,
because copying the real derivation to utsuho needs a signature by a key it
trusts; utsuho runs the genuine article after its own hms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
